title: The scale of the ECI’s deletions in Telangana and Karnataka needs explanation
content_html:
The Special Intensive Revision (SIR) process being conducted by the Election Commission of India (ECI) is increasingly leading to a clear case of disenfranchisement in several parts of India. Marauding on after a judgment by the Supreme Court of India allowed it to proceed, the SIR has now struck out a fifth of the names from the electoral rolls in Telangana and Karnataka — nearly 22% and 19.5% respectively — and among the highest in the country. The cuts are steepest in their capital cities — five constituencies in Bengaluru have lost more than half of their electors while nine of Hyderabad’s 15 have seen deletions of more than 40%. Cuts of this kind cannot simply be a trimming of bloated rolls at the margins. If they are accurate, the ECI’s own summary revision processes were yielding bloated rolls in recent elections, and doing so in the very places with high net in-migration from the rest of India. And if the deletions are to be justified, those struck off the rolls must have left the States — a move within Karnataka or Telangana would only relocate a voter’s name on the same State roll, not remove it altogether. Yet, this is neither borne out by recent survey data nor by the government’s own population estimates.

During the Bihar SIR, the Court asked why political parties had filed so few objections, seeking inclusion of wrongly deleted names; that question might hold true for the Southern States as well. A plausible reason could be that the voter id is useful to a citizen only once in a few years, leading to less alacrity on their part. This may explain why a process that puts the onus on electors yields cuts of this scale. Meanwhile, proving a smoking gun in the data is difficult because of the ECI’s opacity. It has not published the elector-to-population ratio for any State so far during the revision even though doing so is mandatory and is the only test of under-enrolment. The Karnataka Chief Electoral Officer has not even bothered to release a gender-wise breakdown of the deletions, instead scattering the lists across several Google Drive links without the old booth numbers, making verification arduous. The outcome of such shoddiness is visible in West Bengal, where the ECI’s dubious “logical discrepancy” process disenfranchised lakhs of electors, forcing them to seek redress before tribunals set up under the aegis of the Court. Months after the elections, records obtained under a Right to Information request show that barely 82,000 of the nearly 38 lakh appeals before the 19 tribunals have been decided, with more than 90% of those decisions favouring electors seeking restoration. The ECI — an institution once envied even by wealthier democracies for bringing large numbers of Indians to the polling booth — is now an obstacle to universal adult franchise.

title: Injuries are coming in the way of anticipated matchups in US Open
content_html:
The Carlos Alcaraz-Jannik Sinner rivalry is no doubt this era’s defining matchup, but it has also been punctuated by long pauses. In early 2025, Sinner was absent for three months as he served a doping-related ban; this season, Alcaraz was out of action for four months from mid-April owing to a troublesome wrist. Just when it seemed that the two leading lights will come face to face at the US Open starting Sunday, Sinner has been waylaid by a knee injury. In 2025, they met six times in six months; there has just been a solitary duel in the subsequent nine. In a way, the postponement of the battle may suit Alcaraz, for the seven-time Major champion has not played a competitive singles fixture since Barcelona in April. The Spaniard has warmed up for Flushing Meadows with two mixed doubles matches partnering the legendary Serena Williams, but a best-of-five-sets contest is a significant step-up. The 23-year-old will open against Roman Safiullin — a tricky player who beat Alcaraz in 2023 on a Paris hard-court and reached the Wimbledon fourth round this year — and is drawn to meet the in-form American Ben Shelton in the quarterfinal. Potential semifinal opponents include 24-time Slam titlist Novak Djokovic and 2021 US Open winner Daniil Medvedev, which makes the defending champion’s path challenging.

However, Djokovic and Medvedev are on their own tough journeys. The 39-year-old Serb is no longer the once-renowned hard-court master, and lost his lone match – in Cincinnati – after the semifinal reverse to Sinner at Wimbledon. Medvedev was last in a Major final at the 2024 Australian Open and is without a trophy since February. Alexander Zverev thus has a golden opportunity to make his big breakthrough on his favourite surface. Without Sinner, the German will be the top seed, and following the French Open triumph and Wimbledon runner-up finish, the 29-year-old will be confidence personified. Among women, two-time defending champion Aryna Sabalenka would have liked to be that player, but the Belarusian World No. 1 has wobbled of late and seen her lead at the top cut to less than 450 points. Her chief challenger Elena Rybakina may be racing against time to recover from an ankle injury, but with Iga Swiatek, Coco Gauff and Jessica Pegula all in impressive form leading into New York, Sabalenka will have a daunting task. Wimbledon winner Linda Noskova will be looking for a worthy follow-up while the fast-rising 21-year-old from the Philippines, Alexandra Eala, will hope to continue her recent eye-popping run. With Serena and Venus Williams set to pair up in doubles, there will be a rich sprinkling of stardust too.

title: A shared disaster, beyond borders and geopolitics
author: Bhaskar Koirala
content_html:
On Wednesday, August 26, 2026, at approximately 8.44 a.m. Nepal time, what initially appeared to be a 4.4-magnitude earthquake struck near the Nepal-China border. It triggered the collapse of an enormous glacial slab, which plunged a kilometre below to the valley floor, resulting in devastating flash floods. The United States Geological Survey later confirmed that the seismic activity was, in fact, the glacial collapse itself and the landslide (later registered as equivalent to an earthquake measuring 5.2) rather than by tectonic shifts. Preliminary estimates suggest that 579 people have perished in Nepal, with nearly 2,000 people missing, many of them believed to be foreigners.

Entire villages and towns that this writer has previously travelled through have been swept away. Vital infrastructure, such as bridges and hydropower stations, has been completely decimated. A staggering 475 megawatts of generating capacity has been wiped off Nepal’s electricity grid. This may go down as the most devastating natural disaster Nepal has ever witnessed.

Nature’s fury knows no borders

For Nepal and its two neighbours, India and China, which ordinarily see themselves caught up in geopolitical contestations in the country, the catastrophic force of Mother Nature is a reminder that the political dimensions of geography are relevant only insofar as nature does not intervene, unexpectedly and destructively. The natural world does not recognise political boundaries in the same way that the custodians of nation-states do. China and India both suffered substantial losses from Wednesday’s floods. Human and property losses continue to mount in all three countries, including Nepal.

Related Stories

  • Fresh glacial lakes form at source of Nepal’s ice-rock avalanche

  • Glacier break or earthquake? What triggered the Nepal floods? | Explained

  • Nepal floods highlight growing glacier risks in warming Himalayas

China’s Gyirong Port, the largest land trade port in the Tibet Autonomous Region and the primary gateway between Nepal and China, was designated an international-standard land port. An upgrade in August 2017 led to its transformation, upgrading it from a bilateral crossing to a fully recognised international gateway.

Built at a cost of $175.8 million, the port and the services it provided are now effectively buried beneath heavy sediment and debris.

Access roads on the Chinese side leading to the Nepal border, as well as power supplies and local communication links, have been completely severed or severely damaged. There are reports of fatalities on the Chinese side — a number that is almost certain to rise. There are also reports of people missing in Tibet’s Gyirong County, including foreign nationals.

Editorial | Danger from above: On the Nepal flood

The loss of human life for India is tragic, with the Ministry of External Affairs (MEA) confirming that Indian nationals are missing or untraced. Most of them were tourists-cum-pilgrims headed to the abode of Lord Shiva at Kailash Mansarovar. This is a route this writer has travelled on more than a few occasions. The pilgrims would have driven from Kathmandu through the lush, rocky and distinctly narrow river valley to reach Gyirong Port, before proceeding further upwards to the majestic Tibetan Plateau.

Flood fallout for India

For India, the downstream flood threats to its States have been severe, although the immediate threat from some of these events may have passed. Floodwaters reached the Gandak, Kosi and Ganga rivers in Bihar, prompting authorities in Patna to go on maximum alert and deploy large teams, particularly to the Valmikinagar Barrage and along vulnerable embankments, to monitor alarmingly high water levels. Riverside communities were evacuated to safer locations. Authorities in Uttar Pradesh also went on alert, with the State’s Relief Commissioner tracking developments in real time, as overflowing rivers from Nepal naturally flow into Indian territory.

Border districts such as Maharajganj and Kushinagar stepped up emergency surveillance and deployed emergency personnel. India’s National Disaster Response Force (NDRF) deployed teams across the Bihar-Uttar Pradesh border area. New Delhi also activated an extensive Humanitarian Assistance and Disaster Relief programme. The Indian Air Force dispatched more than 47.5 tonnes of emergency relief material to Nepal, including medical supplies, rations and tents.

A case for cooperation

All of this underscores how severely this calamitous event has affected all three countries — Nepal, India and China. The question that arises, therefore, is how to transcend some of the parochial features of geopolitics, while by no means ignoring the compulsions of realpolitik, and create a feasible framework for collaboration and coordination.

There is little doubt that Nepal, India and China will need to effectively address increasingly unpredictable cross-border natural phenomena such as the one we have just witnessed. There is equally little doubt that such events are likely to recur in the future.

The past few days have underscored the need to find ways to compartmentalise the harder political dynamics of the China-India-Nepal relationship and create space for cooperation when confronted with events that remind us of the fickleness of nature, the fragility of human life, and the physical interconnections that inextricably link the three countries.

Bhaskar Koirala is a Nepali scholar based in New Delhi and the founder of the Nepal Institute of International and Strategic Studies, which launched the first Nepal-India-China Trilateral Track II Dialogue in 2014

title: Being bisexual in India is still surprisingly complicated
author: Barry Rodgers
content_html:
There is a peculiar administrative burden to being bisexual. You tell someone you’re bisexual and, almost immediately, they want supplementary documentation. But which do you prefer?Are you sure you’re not gay? Are you sure you’re not straight?

It is remarkable how quickly a statement about your sexuality becomes a customer-service enquiry.

In India in 2026, bisexuality is more visible than it has ever been. Dating apps have given people the vocabulary, popular culture has become more willing to acknowledge sexual fluidity, and younger Indians seem considerably less attached to the idea that attraction must behave itself inside one of two boxes. Tinder’s 2023 India research, based on a survey of 1,000 young Indian daters aged 18–25, found that 33% said their sexual orientation was more fluid than it had been three years earlier, while 56% said they were open to dating people with diverse gender identities, sexual orientations and gender expressions.

That does not mean 33% of young Indians are bisexual. Fluidity and bisexuality aren’t interchangeable. But the number does suggest something has shifted: young people are becoming less convinced that attraction needs to come with a permanent Government-issued certificate.

A friend of mine has identified as bisexual for as long as I’ve known him. He isn’t someone who “discovered” bisexuality after a particularly confusing Saturday night. He has always known. What he has discovered, repeatedly, is that other people find the concept considerably more confusing than he does.

representative image | Photo Credit: Frazao Studio Latino

“With women, there’s always this question of whether I’m actually bi,” he tells me. “They want to know if I’m secretly gay, or if I’m eventually going to leave them for a man.”

With men, he says, the suspicion can go in the other direction. “Some gay men think you’re just not ready to admit you’re gay. And some men hear bisexual and think you’re automatically sexually adventurous.”

His problem isn’t necessarily rejection but the interrogation before the relationship can even begin. “I’m not confused,” he says. “I’m attracted to people.”

Proof in the research

Indian research has been documenting versions of this for years. A 2018 study, Humanizing an Invisible Population in India: Voices from Bisexual Men Concerning Identity, Life Experiences, and Sexual Health, published in the January 2019 issue of Archives of Sexual Behavior, drew on four focus groups involving 22 men and 50 in-depth interviews with self-identified bisexual men in Mumbai. Researchers found secrecy, discretion, family expectations and social pressure shaping how men understood and disclosed their sexuality. Crucially, participants described experiencing stigma from both heterosexual and gay communities.

One participant’s observation about the Bollywood film Dostana was particularly telling: John Abraham’s character could be read as bisexual, but audiences conveniently categorised the two men as gay. It was easier to understand “gay” than to entertain the possibility that attraction might not come with a single destination.

Which is rather the Indian problem in miniature. We are quite happy with categories, but are less comfortable with ambiguity.

Indian cinema has occasionally done better. Margarita with a Straw gave us Laila, played by Kalki Koechlin, a young woman with cerebral palsy who is attracted to both men and women. Academic analyses have specifically examined the film’s bisexuality, disability and challenge to heteronormative ideas about desire.

But bisexuality in popular culture still tends to be presented as a plot point. Real bisexual people are much less cinematic.

My friend in Bengaluru has had longer-term relationships with women but says she has often felt more inclined to hook up with men while having deeper emotional relationships with women. She doesn’t experience this as some internal parliamentary debate about where her sexuality stands this week. It is how attraction has happened for her.

Dating men, however, comes with its own peculiar hazards. “I’m always fetishised,” she tells me. She has repeatedly been propositioned for threesomes. “I’m not open to that,” she says. She says this hasn’t changed much for her “in over a decade”.

representative image | Photo Credit: whitebalance.space

You would imagine that bisexuality would make the dating pool enormous. More genders, more possibilities, and more people. Mathematics would appear to be on your side. Apparently not. A 2022 study, published in the Journal of Homosexuality, Gendered Anti-Bisexual Bias: Heterosexual, Bisexual, and Gay/Lesbian People’s Willingness to Date Sexual Orientation Ingroup and Outgroup Members, surveyed 1,823 participants. Researchers found that heterosexual and gay/lesbian people were less willing to date bisexual people than bisexual people were to date them. The reluctance was particularly strong towards bisexual men, and, notably, even bisexual women showed a preference against dating bisexual men.

My friend has therefore developed his own theory. “Dating bisexual women is easier.” Not necessarily better but more sexually compatible. “There is less explaining,” he says.

A bisexual woman, he believes, already understands that attraction to one gender does not cancel attraction to another. She is less likely to regard a boyfriend’s attraction to men as evidence that he is secretly waiting to leave her. She understands that bisexuality doesn’t mean wanting everyone in the room.

“It’s almost cultish,” he jokes about the little bi-for-bi dating ecosystem that seems to have developed around him.

It is, admittedly, a very niche cult. The initiation ritual is having to explain that bisexual doesn’t mean promiscuous. The secret handshake is comparing notes about the time somebody asked, “But would you actually marry a man?” The central doctrine is simply: please believe me when I tell you who I am.

And there is research to suggest why that relief can matter. A 2020 longitudinal study, Bisexual Men’s Experiences with Discrimination, Internalized Binegativity, and Identity Affirmation: Differences by Partner Gender, followed 180 young bisexual men. The researchers found that bisexual men experienced more interpersonal hostility from heterosexual and gay/lesbian people when their serious partner was a woman. Men with only female sexual partners also encountered more assumptions of sexual irresponsibility from heterosexual people; those with only male partners encountered more assumptions that their sexual orientation was unstable.

Then there is the 50-year-old woman in Kolkata who discovered bisexuality after her marriage dissolved in 2022. She has enjoyed the company of men and women, but rejects the idea that she woke up one morning and selected a new orientation from a dropdown menu.

representative image | Photo Credit: pixdeluxe

“It’s not that you wake up choosing one gender over the other one fine day,” she says. “It’s a basic human connection.” She says she can gravitate towards a man or a woman depending on the person.

“A lot of people think we wake up choosing to like a specific gender,” she says. “I don’t particularly like that.” Her siblings know about her “newfound orientation”. Friends can be another matter.

Not as simple

There is an important difference between being able to say “I’m bisexual” and being able to find other bisexual people. Mainstream apps don’t simply offer a magic show me bisexuals button. Tinder’s orientation information can influence who is surfaced, and Bumble lets you choose the genders you want to date, but neither is quite the bisexual dating concierge one might imagine.

Which means the offline infrastructure matters. And here, things become considerably more scrappy. Delhi has had Bi Collective Delhi, an independent voluntary collective for bisexual, bi+, bi-curious and pansexual people, explicitly designed as a support group and safe space for people attracted to people of their own and other genders.

Mumbai has Umang, the LBT support group of The Humsafar Trust, which includes bisexual women and trans people and has historically run workshops, social events and informal chill outs — gatherings with games and no agenda.

But a dedicated, nationwide offline bisexual social infrastructure is hardly flourishing.

Ask bisexual people in Mumbai where the bisexual events are and the answer can be remarkably bleak. In a 2025 Reddit thread asking specifically about a Mumbai bisexual community and events, commenters said there were no bi-specific events; by February 2026, one commenter described the local scene as “dead”. That’s Reddit, obviously, not a national social survey. But it is a useful little glimpse into the gap between being represented on an app and actually having somewhere to go.

The research on dating bias tells us that bisexual people are still negotiating a world where their sexuality can itself be a disadvantage in the dating market.

A fortnightly guide to love in the age of bare minimum

Indian research has been documenting versions of this for years. A 2018 study, Humanizing an Invisible Population in India: Voices from Bisexual Men Concerning Identity, Life Experiences, and Sexual Health, published in the January 2019 issue of
Archives of Sexual Behavior
, drew on four focus groups involving 22 men and 50 in-depth interviews with self-identified bisexual men in Mumbai. Researchers found secrecy, discretion, family expectations and social pressure shaping how men understood and disclosed their sexuality. Crucially, participants described experiencing stigma from both heterosexual and gay communities.
One participant’s observation about the Bollywood film
Dostana
was particularly telling: John Abraham’s character could be read as bisexual, but audiences conveniently categorised the two men as gay. It was easier to understand “gay” than to entertain the possibility that attraction might not come with a single destination.
Which is rather the Indian problem in miniature. We are quite happy with categories, but are less comfortable with ambiguity.
Indian cinema has occasionally done better.
Margarita with a Straw
gave us Laila, played by Kalki Koechlin, a young woman with cerebral palsy who is attracted to both men and women. Academic analyses have specifically examined the film’s bisexuality, disability and challenge to heteronormative ideas about desire.
But bisexuality in popular culture still tends to be presented as a plot point. Real bisexual people are much less cinematic.
My friend in Bengaluru has had longer-term relationships with women but says she has often felt more inclined to hook up with men while having deeper emotional relationships with women. She doesn’t experience this as some internal parliamentary debate about where her sexuality stands this week. It is how attraction has happened for her.
Dating men, however, comes with its own peculiar hazards. “I’m always fetishised,” she tells me. She has repeatedly been propositioned for threesomes. “I’m not open to that,” she says. She says this hasn’t changed much for her “in over a decade”.
representative image
                                                            | Photo Credit: 
                                whitebalance.space
You would imagine that bisexuality would make the dating pool enormous. More genders, more possibilities, and more people. Mathematics would appear to be on your side. Apparently not. A 2022 study, published in the Journal of Homosexuality, Gendered Anti-Bisexual Bias: Heterosexual, Bisexual, and Gay/Lesbian People’s Willingness to Date Sexual Orientation Ingroup and Outgroup Members, surveyed 1,823 participants. Researchers found that heterosexual and gay/lesbian people were less willing to date bisexual people than bisexual people were to date them. The reluctance was particularly strong towards bisexual men, and, notably, even bisexual women showed a preference against dating bisexual men.
My friend has therefore developed his own theory. “Dating bisexual women is easier.” Not necessarily better but more sexually compatible.  “There is less explaining,” he says.
A bisexual woman, he believes, already understands that attraction to one gender does not cancel attraction to another. She is less likely to regard a boyfriend’s attraction to men as evidence that he is secretly waiting to leave her. She understands that bisexuality doesn’t mean wanting everyone in the room.
“It’s almost cultish,” he jokes about the little bi-for-bi dating ecosystem that seems to have developed around him.
It is, admittedly, a very niche cult. The initiation ritual is having to explain that bisexual doesn’t mean promiscuous. The secret handshake is comparing notes about the time somebody asked, “But would you actually marry a man?” The central doctrine is simply: please believe me when I tell you who I am.
And there is research to suggest why that relief can matter. A 2020 longitudinal study, Bisexual Men’s Experiences with Discrimination, Internalized Binegativity, and Identity Affirmation: Differences by Partner Gender, followed 180 young bisexual men. The researchers found that bisexual men experienced more interpersonal hostility from heterosexual and gay/lesbian people when their serious partner was a woman. Men with only female sexual partners also encountered more assumptions of sexual irresponsibility from heterosexual people; those with only male partners encountered more assumptions that their sexual orientation was unstable.
Then there is the 50-year-old woman in Kolkata who discovered bisexuality after her marriage dissolved in 2022. She has enjoyed the company of men and women, but rejects the idea that she woke up one morning and selected a new orientation from a dropdown menu.
representative image
                                                            | Photo Credit: 
                                pixdeluxe
“It’s not that you wake up choosing one gender over the other one fine day,” she says. “It’s a basic human connection.” She says she can gravitate towards a man or a woman depending on the person.
“A lot of people think we wake up choosing to like a specific gender,” she says. “I don’t particularly like that.” Her siblings know about her “newfound orientation”. Friends can be another matter.
Not as simple
There is an important difference between being able to say “I’m bisexual” and being able to find other bisexual people. Mainstream apps don’t simply offer a magic show me bisexuals button. Tinder’s orientation information can influence who is surfaced, and Bumble lets you choose the genders you want to date, but neither is quite the bisexual dating concierge one might imagine.
Which means the offline infrastructure matters. And here, things become considerably more scrappy. Delhi has had Bi Collective Delhi, an independent voluntary collective for bisexual, bi+, bi-curious and pansexual people, explicitly designed as a support group and safe space for people attracted to people of their own and other genders.
Mumbai has Umang, the LBT support group of The Humsafar Trust, which includes bisexual women and trans people and has historically run workshops, social events and informal chill outs — gatherings with games and no agenda.
But a dedicated, nationwide offline bisexual social infrastructure is hardly flourishing.
Ask bisexual people in Mumbai where the bisexual events are and the answer can be remarkably bleak. In a 2025 Reddit thread asking specifically about a Mumbai bisexual community and events, commenters said there were no bi-specific events; by February 2026, one commenter described the local scene as “dead”. That’s Reddit, obviously, not a national social survey. But it is a useful little glimpse into the gap between being represented on an app and actually having somewhere to go.
The research on dating bias tells us that bisexual people are still negotiating a world where their sexuality can itself be a disadvantage in the dating market.
A fortnightly guide to love in the age of bare minimum

title: Letters to The Editor — August 29, 2026
content_html:
A climate frontline

The disturbing pictures emerging from Nepal and the affected regions show the enormous destruction caused by end-glacial lake outburst floods (EGLOFs) and other extreme natural events.

Rising temperatures, melting glaciers, erratic rainfall and environmental degradation are increasing the vulnerability of the Himalayan regions. Stronger climate policies, sustainable development, protection of forests and rivers, and disaster-preparedness measures are essential. Nepal and its neighbours must act collectively before nature sends even stronger warnings.

Md Sabir Hussain,

Arrah, Bihar

The devastation has exposed the vulnerability of communities living in one of the world’s most fragile mountain ecosystems. It is a grim reminder of how rapidly natural disasters can turn into humanitarian catastrophes. The immediate priority must be rescue, relief and rehabilitation. Saving human lives, however, requires moving from disaster response to disaster prevention. Countries sharing these mountains and glaciers — India, China, Pakistan, Nepal and Bhutan — should coordinate to keep people safe across borders. India and China, in particular, must demonstrate that saving human lives and protecting the environment can transcend political differences.

Gregory Fernandes,

Mumbai

The disaster has prompted explanations, including avalanches, earthquakes, Chinese dam releases, western disturbances, intense rainfall and glacial lake outbursts. Determining the precise cause will require rigorous scientific investigation, although political considerations and inadequate reporting may complicate the assessment. The broader lesson is clear: ecological disruption can intensify natural hazards.

R.S. Narula,

Patiala, Punjab

title: Five years on, Taliban are still at a fork in the road
author: Mahesh Sachdev
content_html:
For a people long regarded as at the crossroads of civilisations, the past five years of the Islamic Emirate of Afghanistan (IEA) under Taliban rule resemble the backwaters. After 47 years of bloodletting, terrorism and foreign occupation, the current “stability” is a respite. But the ongoing time-freeze only postpones an eventual transition to modern universality. So far, the process has been glacial and selective, causing pain and uncertainty. It is time to take stock of the past half-decade and try to fix the broad contours of a foreseeable future.

The IEA’s overall performance since the August 15, 2021 takeover has been a binary. On the positive side, though the IEA 2.0 transition was as chaotic as the IEA 1.0 transition in 1996, it spared the country from mass retribution. Afghanistan is now largely stable and secure. The country’s “Badlands” were long associated with militant groups such as al-Qaeda. Their 9/11 attacks unleashed two decades of bloody U.S. retribution on both al-Qaeda and the IEA 1.0. The IEA 2.0 has disallowed the use of their territory for operations against other countries. During the past five years, an estimated 5.7 million refugees from Pakistan and Iran have returned to Afghanistan. While this return of an eighth of the country’s population has exacerbated the penury, the government has managed it reasonably well. These unmistakable shifts from the ruinous policies of the previous Islamic Emirate (1996-2001) have partially mitigated the world’s concerns.

title: Danger from above: On the Nepal flood
content_html:
Disaster struck Nepal on Wednesday after a flash flood ravaged the Himalayas and foothills. As of Thursday, at least 389 people including several foreign tourists, had died, while at least 300 Indians remained missing. Satellite imagery analysed by global agencies, including the Indian Space Research Organisation, points to a glacier collapse or ice-rock avalanche in Tibet, possibly followed by a temporary river blockage and its sudden failure. An earthquake was initially suspected, but evidence has not borne it out. While the immediate flood wave has passed, there are warnings of possible secondary flooding from debris blockages upstream. There has been extensive damage along the Bhote Koshi and Trishuli corridors, with settlements washed away and hydropower and monitoring infrastructure damaged. Nepalese authorities said 35 motorable and 45 suspension bridges and about 40 kilometres of roads had been damaged.

Given that it is the monsoon, north India and the larger Himalayan regions are under the influence of a powerful Western Disturbance. It would thus not have been unreasonable to attribute the floods to these extratropical storms that can cause clouds to collide with mountains and release enormous quantities of rain at short notice. But the ubiquity of satellites is helping establish a more complex picture, pointing to collapsing glaciers and recalling the October 2023 South Lhonak Lake disaster in Sikkim. There, an eponymous Himalayan glacier suddenly gave way, releasing millions of tonnes of water, debris and rock that pulverised Sikkim’s largest hydropower project. Subsequent analysis showed that the resulting Glacial Lake Outburst Flood (GLOF) had been years in the making. The Indian Himalayas have nearly 7,500 glacial lakes and about 15,000 glaciers, some monitored through remote sensing. Yet, fully assessing their condition requires site visits, difficult because these lakes lie in inhospitable terrain while expeditions are generally feasible only from July to September. Even with satellite monitoring, accurately forecasting a glacier collapse remains exceedingly difficult — and can be counterproductive if warnings trigger panic among residents who, often because of habit or lack of alternatives, are unlikely to move out of harm’s way. Dams and hydropower projects in such terrain are often among the first casualties of these natural outbursts, which are increasing amid global warming. Beyond relief and rescue, governments must enforce construction codes, discourage settlements and large projects in known vulnerable zones, and invest in better tracking of glacier health. Such monitoring can feed long-term disaster planning into development programmes. A tragedy is frequently not the result of a conspiracy but the product of passive neglect; the latter can be addressed.
